title: Indexing
summary: Indexes trade extra writes and space for dramatically faster reads — learn how B+ trees, hashing, and bitmaps work, and when adding an index actually hurts.

blocks.markdown:
An **index** is an auxiliary lookup structure built on one or more columns. Instead of scanning every row, the database jumps straight to matching rows — the same idea as a book's index.

- Indexes live **alongside** the table; they are not the table.
- Trade-off: faster reads, slower writes, extra disk space.
- The database chooses which index to use via the **query optimizer**.
- Most databases auto-create an index on the primary key.

blocks.subTitle: How an index speeds a query
blocks.markdown:
Without an index the engine does a **full table scan** — reads every row to find matches. With an index it:

1. Looks up the search key in the index structure (cheap, O(log n) or O(1)).
2. Follows a pointer to the exact disk page.
3. Reads only that page.

**Selectivity** — the fraction of rows a predicate matches. A highly selective predicate (few matches) benefits most from an index.

**Primary (clustering) index** — built on the column that physically orders the file on disk. There can be only one, because the file can have only one physical order. Lookups are very fast.

**Secondary (non-clustering) index** — built on any other column. The rows are NOT in that order on disk, so each pointer may land on a different disk page (**random I/O**). Useful but more expensive per lookup.

blocks.subTitle: Clustered vs non-clustered (SQL Server / MySQL terms)
blocks.markdown:
| | Clustered | Non-clustered |
|---|---|---|
| Rows stored | In index order | Elsewhere |
| Count per table | 1 | Many |
| Range scans | Very fast | Slower (random I/O) |

In MySQL InnoDB every table has exactly one clustered index (the primary key). Other indexes are non-clustered. See [sql-objects](sql-objects).

**Dense index** — one index entry per data record. Always points directly to the record; works on any file order.

**Sparse index** — one entry per **disk block**, not per record. Only works if records are sorted by the index key. Uses far less space, but a lookup may need a short scan inside the block.

A primary index is often sparse; secondary indexes are always dense.

When the index itself is large, searching it requires many I/Os. The fix: build a **sparse outer index on top of the inner index** — a multi-level index.

- Each level reduces the search space by the **fan-out** (entries per node).
- **Fan-out** = number of child pointers a single index node holds. High fan-out → fewer levels → fewer I/Os.
- This idea is the foundation of B-trees.

blocks.subTitle: The B-tree
blocks.markdown:
A **B-tree** (balanced tree) generalizes a binary search tree to have many children per node (high fan-out), keeping the tree short.

- Every internal node holds keys AND data pointers — you can find a record at any level.
- Nodes are sized to match a **disk page** (typically 4–16 KB), minimizing I/Os.
- All paths from root to leaf have the same length — always balanced.
- Insertion/deletion rebalance automatically via node splits and merges.

blocks.subTitle: Why B+ tree wins
blocks.markdown:
The **B+ tree** (used by nearly every real RDBMS) makes one key change: **only leaf nodes hold data pointers**; internal nodes hold only keys as routing guides.

- Internal nodes can fit far more keys → even higher fan-out → shallower tree.
- All leaf nodes are **linked in a sorted chain** → range scans are one traversal to the start, then a sequential walk along leaves.
- Result: point lookups and range queries are both fast.

Most production indexes (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle, SQL Server) are B+ trees.

blocks.subTitle: Static hashing
blocks.markdown:
**Static hashing** maps a search key to a **bucket** via a fixed hash function `h(key) mod N`. Lookups are O(1) on average.

- Problem: if `N` is fixed and data grows, buckets overflow → long **overflow chains** → slow scans.
- Also wastes space when data shrinks.
- Good only when the data size is known and stable.

blocks.subTitle: Dynamic hashing
blocks.markdown:
Dynamic hashing lets the structure **grow and shrink** with data.

- **Extendible hashing** — uses a **global depth** (bits of the hash examined) and a directory that can double when needed. Only split buckets that are full.
- **Linear hashing** — splits buckets in a fixed round-robin order regardless of which overflows; no directory. Simpler but less precise.

Both avoid hash indexes becoming a mess as data volume changes.

A **bitmap index** stores, for each distinct value of a column, a bit vector — one bit per row, 1 if that row has the value.

- Ideal for **low-cardinality** columns (few distinct values): `gender`, `status`, `region`. **Cardinality** = number of distinct values.
- AND/OR operations between bitmaps are very fast (bitwise CPU ops).
- Terrible for high-cardinality columns (e.g., `user_id`) — one huge bitmap per distinct value.
- Common in data warehouses (OLAP), not in OLTP.

A **covering index** is an index that contains every column a query needs — so the database never touches the table at all.

Example: query selects `name, salary` and filters on `dept_id`. An index on `(dept_id, name, salary)` **covers** it — the answer is fully in the index.

- Eliminates the extra I/O of going back to the table (called a **heap fetch**).
- Powerful for read-heavy, repeated queries. Trade-off: larger index.

See [query-processing-optimization](query-processing-optimization).

blocks.subTitle: Creating an index in SQL
blocks.markdown:
```sql
-- Basic index on one column
CREATE INDEX idx_emp_dept ON employees(dept_id);

-- Covering index for a specific query pattern
CREATE INDEX idx_emp_dept_cover
  ON employees(dept_id, name, salary);

-- Unique index (enforces uniqueness + speeds lookups)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_emp_email
  ON employees(email);
```

Drop with `DROP INDEX idx_emp_dept;`. See [sql-objects](sql-objects) for full DDL.

More indexes ≠ better. Indexes hurt when:

- **Write overhead** — every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must update all indexes on that table.
- **Low selectivity** — an index on a boolean column (50/50 split) often makes the optimizer just do a table scan anyway.
- **Too many indexes** — the optimizer spends time choosing; the storage bloats; writes slow down.
- **Small tables** — a scan of a 1000-row table is cheaper than an index lookup + pointer follow.
- **Bulk loads** — dropping indexes before a bulk insert, then rebuilding, is often faster.

blocks.subTitle: Index summary
blocks.markdown:
| Index type | Best for | Avoid when |
|---|---|---|
| B+ tree | Range + point, most queries | Write-heavy, tiny tables |
| Hash | Exact match only | Range queries |
| Bitmap | Low-cardinality OLAP | High-cardinality, OLTP writes |

blocks.subTitle: Why B+ tree over binary tree or hash
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why do databases use B+ trees instead of binary search trees or hash indexes?**

A binary tree has fan-out 2 → very deep → many disk I/Os. A B+ tree node holds hundreds of keys → tree is only 3–4 levels deep for millions of rows → very few I/Os. Hash indexes answer exact-match in O(1) but **cannot do range queries** (`BETWEEN`, `>`, `ORDER BY`). B+ trees do both, which is why they back almost every production index.

Key phrase: **high fan-out keeps the tree shallow; linked leaves enable range scans**.

blocks.subTitle: Clustered vs non-clustered
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?**

A **clustered** index dictates the physical storage order of rows. Because matching rows are adjacent on disk, range scans are very fast. One per table.

A **non-clustered** index stores key+pointer separately; the rows sit in their own heap. Each pointer may land on a different disk page (random I/O). Many allowed per table.

Rule of thumb: use the clustered index on the column you range-scan most (often the primary key or a date).

blocks.subTitle: When do indexes slow you down?
blocks.markdown:
**Q: When would adding an index actually slow the database down?**

Every write (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) must update every index on the table. If a table has many indexes and is write-heavy (OLTP transactions), the overhead adds up. Also:

- **Low selectivity** — index on a column that's almost always the same value; optimizer ignores it anyway.
- **Small tables** — scan cost < index lookup cost.
- **Bulk loads** — rebuilding one index at the end beats incremental updates on many indexes.

Index everything = index nothing useful.

blocks.subTitle: What is a covering index?
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is a covering index and why is it powerful?**

A covering index includes all columns that a specific query needs to read. The engine answers the query entirely from the index — it never touches the main table (no heap fetch). This eliminates one I/O round-trip per row. It is one of the highest-impact tuning techniques for read-heavy workloads: add the right extra columns to an existing index and a slow query can become instant.

blocks.subTitle: Dense vs sparse; static vs dynamic hashing
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Dense vs sparse index — when would you use each?**

**Dense** — one entry per record. Always works, but large. Use when the file is unsorted (secondary indexes).

**Sparse** — one entry per block. Only works on sorted files, but much smaller. Use as the primary index on a sorted file or as the outer level of a multilevel index.

**Q: Static vs dynamic hashing?**

Static: fixed bucket count, fast but degrades as data grows (overflow chains). Dynamic (extendible/linear): bucket count grows with data, stays efficient — preferred when data volume changes.
